reference_calls.source_slice: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming,
a bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital,
London,
returned from holiday to find that a stray mould had contaminated a dish of staphylococcus bacteria.
Popular mythology blames an open window;
the spores probably originated in a laboratory downstairs,
where a colleague cultivated moulds.
Yet the crude juice was unstable and stubbornly hard to purify,
and he and the chemists he enlisted lacked the expertise to refine it.
He used it chiefly to isolate other microbes,
and penicillin lay dormant,
a curiosity rather than a cure.
A decade later,
in Oxford,
Howard Florey,
an Australian pathologist,
revived the work with Ernst Chain,
a German-born chemist and Jewish refugee.
On 25 May 1940 eight mice received a lethal dose of bacteria;
only the four also injected with penicillin lived.
The Lancet,
a prestigious journal,
printed the outcome that August.
In February 1941 Albert Alexander,
an Oxford constable gravely ill with infection,
rallied on penicillin.
When the scarce supply ran out,
he died in March:
the obstacle was quantity.
From July 1941 a government laboratory in Peoria,
Illinois,
boosted yields about tenfold with corn-steep liquor,
a starch by-product;
later a mouldy market melon furnished the laboratory with a more prolific strain.
In October 1945 Fleming,
Florey,
and Chain shared the Nobel prize;
Heatley was overlooked.
Fortune put the mould in Fleming's dish;
tenacious teams and years of toil transformed it into a remedy.
